vignette: The rain begins in late October, the same season it did fifteen years ago. At sixty-eight, Elias stands on the tiled roof of his coastal home, watching the storm surge swallow the lower streets of his Latin American hometown. The wind presses against the house like a living weight. He pulls Rosa to the center of the roof, his arms wrapped around her as the water breaches the seawall. Beneath them, the plumbing groans. Inside, the water rises past their knees. He watches the exact moment his neighbor's door tears free from its hinges and drifts into the current. He holds Rosa's hand until his fingers go numb, whispering in Spanish, counting breaths, waiting for the orange flashes of the coast guard boats. When they finally come, he steps into the inflatable hull with the stiff gait of a man who has forgotten how to bend. The months that follow are quiet. He helps Rosa replant the garden, replaces the rotted floorboards, and returns to his desk as a QA Engineer. For decades, his work is a sanctuary of predictable logic. He tests software the way he lives: methodically, looking for the fault before it causes a system failure. But the storm leaves invisible cracks in his routine. He checks the weather applications before opening his eyes each morning. He installs heavier locks on the windows, then double-checks them an hour later. When the sky turns the bruised purple of that October night, he pauses his code reviews, his cursor hovering over the trackpad while his pulse climbs. He tells himself he is being prudent. He tells himself he is just being a good husband, keeping her safe. As the years pass, the vigilance deepens. At seventy-five, he still consults remotely, walking younger engineers through test scenarios with a calm that feels performative even to him. He notices how quickly his mind maps structural vulnerabilities in any room he enters. He counts exits. He runs mental simulations of pipe failures, roof collapses, evacuation bottlenecks. The logic that once brings him quiet satisfaction now serves as a barrier against panic. He reads engineering forums late at night, searching for reassurance that the buildings he passes are sound. Sleep fractures into fragments. He wakes at the same hour, convinced he hears the grinding hum of the flood pumps that never activate. The silence afterward is heavier than the noise ever is. Rosa has learned the geography of his tension. She leaves a mug of café de olla on his desk and sits nearby, reading, understanding that his need for control is a quiet rebellion against the helplessness he feels on that roof. She never mentions the old photos of the flooded street. She never asks why he checks the basement sump pump twice when a warning siren sounds in the distance. Last week, a summer squall knocks out the neighborhood power. Elias retrieves the heavy flashlight, walks to the utility panel, and cycles every breaker. His breathing remains shallow until the refrigerator's compressor kicks back on. He returns to his chair, places his hands flat on the desk, and watches the rain slow. He does not tell Rosa that he counts the drops for the first ten minutes, measuring them like test metrics, trying to prove that this storm, too, has an end. He breathes. He waits. He continues.
